summary: God speaks from the Tent of Meeting and gives Israel instructions for a burnt offering. The chapter follows three possible animals—from the herd, from the flock, or from birds—and assigns the offerer and the priests distinct parts in presenting each one.
whyItMatters: This opening chapter establishes the book's careful attention to access, sacrifice, blood, and priestly service before later chapters introduce other kinds of offerings.

context.author: The chapter presents these instructions as words Yahweh gives to Moses; it does not identify the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: The children of Israel, with specific duties assigned to anyone bringing an offering and to Aaron's sons, the priests.
context.date: The narrative setting is Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: At the Tent of Meeting, with the altar at its entrance and the camp surrounding the sanctuary.
context.literaryForm: Ritual instruction arranged as three parallel cases: herd, flock, and birds.

outline.heading: God addresses Israel through Moses
outline.note: The opening names the place of speech and the broad categories of livestock that may be offered.

outline.heading: A burnt offering from the herd
outline.note: The offerer presents, identifies with, kills, skins, and washes; the priests handle the blood, altar, and fire.

outline.heading: A burnt offering from the flock
outline.note: The sheep-or-goat procedure closely repeats the pattern used for an animal from the herd.

outline.heading: A burnt offering of birds
outline.note: The priest handles a turtledove or pigeon at the altar according to a shorter procedure.

keyVerses.text: “‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The first case states the required condition of the animal, the place of presentation, and the goal of acceptance.

keyVerses.text: He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
keyVerses.why: This verse connects the offerer's gesture with the offering's acceptance and atoning purpose.

keyVerses.text: but he shall wash its innards and its legs with water. The priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: After the hide is removed, the prepared pieces, head, fat, washed innards, and legs are all assigned to the altar fire.

themes: shared duties of offerer and priest
one pattern across three animal types

questions.question: What is a burnt offering in this chapter?
questions.answer: It is an animal offering whose prepared portions are burned on the altar. In the herd case the hide is removed before the pieces are arranged, and in the bird case the crop and feathers are discarded; all three procedures end by calling the offering a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.

questions.question: Who does what when an animal from the herd is offered?
questions.answer: The offerer brings the animal, lays a hand on it, kills it, skins it, cuts it up, and washes specified parts. Aaron's sons present and sprinkle the blood, arrange the fire and pieces, and burn the offering on the altar.

questions.question: What does laying a hand on the animal's head mean here?
questions.answer: The offerer is told to place one hand on the bull before killing it, and verse 4 links the offering with acceptance and atonement. Readers have taken the gesture as transferring guilt or as identifying this animal as the person’s offering; the chapter does not explicitly describe a transfer. The designation reading fits the action stated here without making it the only possible interpretation.

questions.question: What does atonement mean within this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says the burnt offering is accepted to make atonement for the person who brings it. In this immediate setting, the term describes the offering's role in making approach to God acceptable; the chapter does not provide a complete theory of how atonement works.

questions.question: Why must an animal from the herd or flock be male and without defect?
questions.answer: That is the stated requirement for the herd and flock cases. The chapter repeatedly specifies it but does not explain why those features are required, so the safest reading distinguishes the rule itself from later interpretations of its purpose.

questions.question: Why is blood handled separately from the rest of the animal?
questions.answer: In both livestock procedures, the priests sprinkle the blood around the altar while the animal’s pieces are arranged and burned. This chapter establishes that separation and the priests’ role as part of the rite but does not explain the blood’s significance further.

questions.question: Does “a pleasant aroma to Yahweh” mean God needs the smell of food?
questions.answer: The phrase closes all three procedures, while verse 3 separately says the herd animal is brought so the offerer may be accepted before Yahweh. The chapter associates the completed rite with favorable reception, but it never says that God is fed by the offering or physically depends on its smoke.

questions.question: What changes when the offering is a bird?
questions.answer: A priest, rather than the offerer, performs the killing and most of the preparation at the altar. The crop and feathers are removed, the bird is torn open without being divided, and the remaining bird is burned as the same kind of offering.

glossary.def: An animal offering whose prepared portions are consumed on the altar under the herd, flock, or bird procedure.
Here, the result by which the offered animal makes the worshiper's approach acceptable before God.
Israel's portable sanctuary and the place from which God addresses Moses at the chapter's opening.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: Exodus closes with the completed Tent of Meeting filled by God’s glory, so Moses cannot enter it (Exodus 40:34–35). Leviticus opens with God calling to Moses from that Tent and directing him to speak to Israel.

here.text: The opening speech gives one burnt-offering procedure in three animal cases: herd, flock, and birds. It distinguishes what the offerer does from what the priests handle at the altar.

after.text: The next chapter turns from animal offerings to flour and prepared grain, with a burned memorial portion and a priestly remainder.
